yu58te.text: Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries have disrupted 57 illegal streaming services that operated hundreds of websites and drew over 7.3 million visits each year. Such illegal IPTV services offer access to television channels, live sports, and movies without permission from the copyright owners for a small monthly fee. According to the European Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA) trade association, legitimate service providers lose around €4.83 billion annually as roughly 60 million people in Europe use illegal platforms for streaming content. "The operation resulted in the disruption of 57 illegal IPTV services and the identification of 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, with a combined annual traffic of more than 7.3 million visits. Investigators have so far traced over EUR 26 million in cryptocurrency transactions, with further analysis ongoing," Europol said in a Tuesday press release. "The operation targeted a criminal market worth billions of euros annually, in which illegal streaming providers sell unauthorised access to premium television channels, live sports and films, often collecting subscription payments through cryptocurrency." As part of this joint action, which also involved Europol, the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, and AAPA, the investigators also partnered with crypto industry experts from Binance, Coinbase, and Chainalysis to trace cryptocurrency payments and identify the financial networks powering these illegal IPTV services. They did this by looking for links between the illegal IPTV services, crypto wallets, financial transactions, and the individuals who control these services, who used the wallets to receive and transfer payments, making it easier to move money between countries and hide the origin of their profits. Europol and the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) joined forces in 2016 to create the Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition (IPC3), which operates within Europol and targets counterfeiting and online and offline piracy. In June, another major international operation coordinated by Bulgaria with Europol's support, dubbed "Operation KRATOS 2," resulted in the removal of more than 27,000 illegal streaming URLs, the shutdown of nine organized crime groups, and 29 arrests. That followed Operation KRATOS, another international anti-piracy operation carried out in summer 2024, which shut down a massive illegal streaming network with over 22 million users worldwide. Earlier this year, in January, Europol, Eurojust, and Interpol also coordinated Operation Switch Off, a global law enforcement action that led to the seizure of three industrial-scale illegal IPTV services. More recently, in May, Italian authorities dismantled the CINEMAGOAL piracy platform, which provided illegal access to many online streaming platforms, including Netflix, Spotify, and Disney+. 1vbfli7.text: Written by: George Manuelian, Chief Strategy Officer, RapidFort The modern software stack has become an iceberg. The application code customers and security teams see at the surface is only a small portion of what is being shipped. Beneath it sit operating systems, frameworks, libraries, packages, and transitive dependencies, with much of it drawn from open source or third parties. As AI accelerates software development, that hidden complexity has become an even more critical security challenge. For business and technology leaders, the question is no longer simply how many vulnerabilities exist. It is where does meaningful risk live, which vulnerabilities can be exploited in our environment, and how we can reduce that risk without turning developers into full-time vulnerability managers. The answer requires a fundamental shift from vulnerability accumulation to continuous software resilience. First step: Recognizing composition of modern software The typical containerized stack is layers of base operating system software, packages, libraries, language frameworks and dependencies, and the application itself. The application a company writes may represent only a small portion of what it ultimately ships. That is important because vulnerabilities multiply. A vulnerable package in a base image is not necessarily one vulnerability in practice; it can be replicated across every application and container that uses that image. In light of this, executives should ask a different question of their security programs: How much of the reported risk is relevant to the way our software operates? Traditional scanning frequently identifies the presence of a vulnerable component without establishing whether that component is loaded, executing, reachable or exposed. A software bill of materials (SBOM) identifies what exists; a runtime bill of materials (RBOM) can pinpoint what is actually being used. That distinction can dramatically reduce noise. For example, in the real world from a customer, an NGINX image containing 152 packages and 48 CVEs had only 47 packages actually running in the application. More than 80% of the software was not being exercised. The lesson is not that every unused package is harmless, but that security teams need operational context before assigning remediation urgency. This is also why severity alone has become an inadequate basis for prioritization. A high or critical Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score can command attention, but the business question is whether the vulnerable code is relevant and exploitable in the environment. There are four contextual factors increasingly shaping remediation decisions: Whether a vulnerability is exposed, whether it is a known exploited vulnerability, whether exploitation is automatable, and whether exploitation would have meaningful technical impact. The shift from severity to exploitability and reachability is important because it changes the operating model. Instead of asking engineering teams to chase the largest number on a scanner dashboard, leaders should ask whether the organization has enough visibility to determine what is running, what is reachable, and what is exposed. As a result, security becomes a business-risk exercise rather than a race to close tickets. Hardening is the important next step Hardening should not mean merely passing a configuration benchmark. It should also mean removing software and functionality that the application does not need . Every unnecessary library, shell, package manager, build utility, or default component increases the amount of software that must be maintained and potentially gives an attacker additional tools if a container is compromised. Runtime profiling is a proven approach for identifying these unused components and removing them systematically. AI makes this discipline more important AI-assisted development can rapidly generate code and pull in packages, but developers may not always know which dependencies were introduced or whether they remain necessary as the application evolves. For example, a development environment in which developers may have to ask the AI system which Python version or packages were used because the model generated much of the implementation is a warning sign for governance. Speed of development cannot come at the expense of knowing what is being shipped. No one is going to slow AI development. The answer is to put security controls into the pipeline so developers do not have to perform every security task manually. Clean, curated base images; runtime profiling; removal of unused components; vulnerability context; and automated rebuilding can become repeatable parts of CI/CD. The objective is to make the secure path the default path. Introducing Zero Trust software architecture Zero Trust has traditionally been associated with network access and identity. But when organizations continuously ingest open source and third-party software, they also need to question the software entering their environments. Software should be verified, trusted components should be maintained in controlled registries, and the software should be continuously evaluated as it moves through development, testing and production – following the common principles of Zero Trust. This represents a meaningful change in how software supply chain security should be managed. The goal should not be a perfect vulnerability dashboard. The goal should be a development system that continuously produces software with less unnecessary code, fewer meaningful vulnerabilities, and a smaller attack surface. For example, one customer reduced an initial 5,286 findings to three unresolved vulnerabilities within 48 hours by combining profiling, curated images, and removal of unused components. The strategic lesson learned Vulnerability remediation should become a manufacturing process, not a recurring emergency. If organizations wait until a scanner produces a massive backlog, they have already allowed complexity to become technical debt. If instead they control what enters the software supply chain, understand what actually runs, prioritize based on reachability and impact, remove what is unnecessary, and continuously rebuild from cleaner components, security becomes part of software production itself. This approach also changes the conversation between security and engineering. Developers should not be expected to fix every finding simply because a scanner found it. They need context, automation and a clear understanding of which risks require action. Security leaders need visibility into runtime behavior and the ability to distinguish a theoretical exposure from a vulnerability that can actually affect the business. The future of software security in the AI era The future of software security belongs to organizations that manage complexity continuously. AI will accelerate development, it’s a given. Open source will remain foundational, that’s understood. Neither trend is going away, nor should it of course. But both make it more important to establish disciplined software intake, strong supply-chain controls, runtime visibility, effective hardening, and automated remediation. Ultimately, the objective is not simply to reduce the number of CVEs on a report. It is to build software that contains less unnecessary functionality, relies on cleaner components, exposes fewer opportunities to attackers, and can be continuously refreshed without overwhelming those responsible for delivering it . Software supply chain security works best when profiling, verification, clean images, and removal of unused components are built directly into the pipeline. The executive mandate for the AI era must stop treating vulnerability management as a downstream cleanup exercise. Build security into the way software is assembled, tested and deployed. When continuous remediation becomes part of the normal development life cycle, organizations can move faster without accepting vulnerability volume as an unavoidable cost of innovation. Eliminate Attack Vectors at the Source. Contact us today to find out more. Sponsored and written by RapidFort.

19rcqxt.text: The federal cybersecurity agency is giving U.S. government departments until Thanksgiving to patch a vulnerability impacting a critical email security platform that blocks spam, malware and other threats. All federal agencies were urged to patch CVE-2026-134624 – a bug affecting N-able’s Mail Assure platform. The vulnerability carries a 9.3 severity score and was added to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) exploited vulnerabilities platform on Monday evening. N-able has dealt with a week of outages tied to the vulnerability after hackers breached one of the company’s servers through the bug, causing damage to Mail Assure and SpamExperts services. In a statement to Recorded Future News, N-able said it remediated the bug over the weekend and restored access to internal dashboards for customers. Inbound and outbound email flow and spam filtering continued to operate throughout the incident, they added. “Since completing these remediation actions, we have continued scanning and monitoring the Mail Assure environments and have found no evidence of exploitation beyond the single N-able-hosted server identified in our initial investigation,” a spokesperson said, adding that they hired incident responders to validate their findings. The company pledged to publish a root cause analysis within the next two weeks. N-able said the breach and service issues are not connected to more than 30 vulnerabilities impacting its N-central platform that were publicicized two weeks ago by a security researcher. N-central is a popular remote management tool that thousands of IT teams use to monitor and run networks remotely. N-able took all hosted N-central environments offline and ordered customers to turn off their servers. A bug in the company’s N-central platform was involved in a supply-chain attack by ransomware actors in August. N-able was previously a business unit within software company SolarWinds before it was spun off as a separate cloud-based software solutions company offering tools to managed service providers.

1j92eyv.text: McDonald's Japan, the fast-food giant's Japanese subsidiary, has disclosed a data breach after attackers accessed a database containing sensitive information for users of the company's official smartphone app. Founded in 1940, McDonald's is now a multinational fast-food chain that operates more than 40,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries and serves tens of millions of customers daily. In a Friday statement, the company's Japanese subsidiary confirmed that threat actors gained access to its official app's database and said the exposed information includes the users' product purchase history, IP addresses, mobile device location data, and customer management IDs (which cannot be used to identify the customers' email addresses or member IDs). McDonald's Japan also added that the exposed data doesn't include the affected customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, or credit card information. While it has yet to reveal when it detected the attack or how many individuals had their data stolen, the company said a follow-up investigation found no service disruption or misuse of official apps as a result of the incident. "We are working to invalidate any credentials used for unauthorized access, investigate the relevant systems, and report to the Personal Information Protection Commission," it said. "In addition, we will strive to strengthen security measures and prevent recurrence." This isn't the first data breach to affect McDonald's in recent years, with the fast food giant disclosing a breach in June 2021 after attackers breached its systems and stole information belonging to employees and customers from the US, South Korea, and Taiwan. In 2017, McDonald's also patched a cross-site scripting (XSS) security flaw that affected its official website and exposed customers' plain-text passwords. Japanese companies under attack Last month, Burger King Japan also disclosed a major data breach after attackers stole 11.18 million customer records that were later leaked online. The two incidents affecting the two Japanese fast food chains add to a large wave of cyberattacks impacting high-profile Japanese companies since the start of the year, including Japan Airlines, entertainment system maker Daiichi Kosho, cloud and digital infrastructure firm IDC Frontier, Japanese publishing giant Nikkei, cloud and data center service provider Sakura Internet, taxi operator Nihon Kotsu, telecommunications giant KDDI, and many others. Macnica researcher Yutaka Sejiyama has logged 288 cybersecurity incidents affecting Japanese organizations involving personal information theft or exposure since the start of the year. Sejiyama found that attackers are now probing websites and APIs for access-control, configuration, and authentication weaknesses, and exploiting known (n-day) vulnerabilities to find other victims. 1d5sbl.text: OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo that deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators prepare and roll out patches, without restarting services. Shirudo leverages the eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) mechanism in Linux to monitor for suspicious activity and deploy targeted protections called "shields." eBPF is a Linux technology that lets programs run in a controlled environment within the operating system's kernel without modifying its source code or requiring a restart. It enables real-time monitoring of system and network activity, performance analysis, and enforcement of targeted security protections, making it an ideal operational basis for Shirudo. Shirudo’s shields aim to block malicious behavior in a targeted way, leaving legitimate application operations undisturbed. OpenAI highlights four core capabilities for the tool: Live protection: Blocks vulnerable code paths without restarting systems, letting operators assess shield impact before enforcing them. AI-assisted defense: Enables agents to investigate vulnerabilities, develop shields, and validate their effectiveness, with deployment remaining under human control. Trusted deployment: Uses cryptographic signatures, Linux's eBPF verifier, and kernel security controls to prevent unauthorized modifications. Hardware-backed verification: Uses Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) to provide verifiable records of shields being loaded or removed. OpenAI and Cisco researchers tested custom-generated shields and demonstrated that they could successfully block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without interrupting its operation. Marcus Hutchins, principal threat researcher at managed detection and response company Expel, says that while there is "genuinely so much runtime exploit mitigation potential with eBPF," it may not be a good idea to let AI agents write rules that could impact the kernel. He also noted that the tool's "capabilities are limited to Linux because Mac/Windows haven't implement the components needed to be effective." Researchers at Isovalent, a cloud networking and security company acquired by Cisco in 2024, explain that "Shirudo is a rewrite of Tetragon," an open-source eBPF-based runtime security platform the company introduced in 2022, which also serves as the foundation for Cisco's existing Live Protect technology. Shirudo is designed for agentic control plane, and a configurable degree of autonomy when it comes to deploying mitigations. Isovalent says the tool isn’t limited to eBPF and can also modify application or userspace runtime bytecode to extend protection where needed. When a shield is deployed, they also provide operators with hit counts, giving them insight into attempted exploits and where defenses need strengthening. Reporting hits on deployed shields Source: Isovalent The two companies plan to provide “ready-to-use” mitigations in the form of tested shields, along with vulnerability disclosures, until patching is possible. Shields will be distributed as cryptographically signed ‘.bee’ packages through an OCI registry. Shirudo's functional overview Source: Isovalent Isovalent says that Shirudo can be activated through a command-line interface and doesn’t require a daemon to run permanently on the machine. "The Shirudo project is only the beginning, but it already shows the true potential of combining agents as a workforce with machine interfaces to let agents output what they are best at: code," the researchers say. They expect the tool to evolve and other projects to emerge around it, to the point of building self-defending that can run applications and agents side by side. Shirudo is open-source (BSD + GPL) and comes with a quick-start guide as well as "getting started" documentation from Isovalent. In a deep-dive webinar on December 15, OpenAI will provide a technical rundown of how the tool works and how it combines eBPF and artificial intelligence to detect and counter new attacks. 191ekr.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 24, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication. The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir"). "A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today. The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam, XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw. Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5). The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5). The issues have been addressed in the following versions - VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2 VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300 VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract) VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - Fixed in 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) The fixes arrive days after Broadcom shipped updates for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), another authentication bypass flaw impacting the VMware Directory Service that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group called Armory Castle. VMware has noted that CVE-2026-123903 is a distinct issue and is not related to CVE-2026-123890. While Broadcom makes no mention of any of the newly disclosed flaws as being exploited in the wild, it's essential that customers apply the updates for optimal protection.

1h4o26o.text: A threat cluster previously assessed to be affiliated with the ShinyHunters extortion crew may have rebranded and continued operations under a new name called INCEPTION, according to Okta's Threat Intelligence team. The cluster, dubbed O-UNC-053, is characterized by the use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Okta said it's been tracking the group since March 2026. The identity and access management provider said targets of this cluster previously had stolen data published to the ShinyHunters data leak site (DLS). However, as of November 16, 2026, a new data leak site operating under the name INCEPTION has listed the data siphoned from O-UNC-053 targets. "While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion," Okta researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said in a report shared with The Hacker News. Social engineering and credential harvesting attacks mounted by O-UNC-053 have targeted a broad range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, biotechnology, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality, and legal. Similar to O-UNC-066 and UNC6671, the newly identified cluster also relies on a phishing kit to intercept authentication flows and capture a user's credentials and MFA codes. However, the kit is not designed to bypass phishing-resistant methods like passkeys and Okta FastPass. "While interacting with targeted users on the phone, the operators socially engineer them into sharing factors like one-time passcodes and approving push notifications," Okta said. "If successful, the operators gain access to SaaS applications and exfiltrate sensitive data, which is often used to extort targets under the threat of releasing it on a data leak site." Domains created by the group are registered through NiceNIC, Spaceship, Tucows, and NameSilo, with the domain names using the following patterns - legal-<target>[.]com legaldept-<target>[.]com <target>[.]legal <target>-legal[.]com The use of "legal" themes in these attacks is said to have started in October 2026, and is often registered on or within a day of a campaign starting. Prior campaign waves have employed help desk-, support-, and claims-related themes for the registered domains. These findings also dovetail with an alert from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which has warned of widespread vishing activity using legal-themed domains that either begin with "legal-" or end with "-legal" using the ".com" top-level domain. More than 70 such domains have been observed since October 2026, it said, adding each domain is specifically created for an intended target operating in different industries, like cryptocurrency, financial services, healthcare, high technology, and hospitality, among others. "Registered in rapid evening batches and shielded behind Cloudflare, these web-only domains deploy a filtered kit that delivers tailored content to intended victims while routing visitors it is not configured to attack to the targeted organization's legitimate Okta or NetIQ sign-in flow," ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons said. Some of the confirmed domains linked to the activity are listed below - legal-pepsico[.]com legal-paychex[.]com legal-duolingo[.]com activisionblizzard-legal[.]com legal-westernunion[.]com legal-dropbox[.]com legal-indeed[.]com legal-creditkarma[.]com legal-amd[.]com legal-grubhub[.]com legal-twitch[.]tv The crux of the campaign is to tailor the landing page to the specific identity provider of the target, while filtering unwanted visitors and forwarding them to the organization's authentication infrastructure, such as Okta. "Throughout our tracking of O-UNC-053 between March and September 2026, we observed the names of targeted entities appear on the ShinyHunters DLS between 1 and 28 days after the phishing infrastructure was registered," Okta noted. However, it's unclear at this stage if the published data on the INCEPTION site is authentic and whether they are running the site themselves or are collaborating with another extortion gang. The exact nature of the relationship between ShinyHunters and O-UNC-053 is also unknown. It's worth noting that the ShinyHunters data leak site went offline in late September 2026 following the arrest of three alleged members of the group, including a Canadian co-conspirator responsible for the breach of the FBIjobs.gov portal. There is no evidence of data from O-UNC-053 targets being published on any data leak site from early September 2026 through October and early November 2026, until listings for multiple targets appeared on the INCEPTION site last week. "This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors," Okta said. "Regardless of the nature of the relationship with the INCEPTION DLS, O-UNC-053 remains active in conducting vishing attacks against targets in an effort to take over accounts, steal data, and extort targets."

1wvbpq4.text: The Hacker NewsNov 24, 2026Supply Chain Security / DevSecOps Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it. In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check. The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it. The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it. That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't. Immutability Is Not Provenance Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected. GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it. But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered: Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned. Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project. Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen. With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely. GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job. GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later. That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server. Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you. What You'll Learn Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers: What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions Who Should Attend Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you. Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either. Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

16c1pii.text: A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday. The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398. Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared. VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework. The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face. The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects. To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis. Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox." The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host. The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image. The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it. "This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced. The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet. Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks. The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights. The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE. What to patch On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it. .NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694. Flaw Affected Fixed in CVE-2026-87268 (VirtualBox) VirtualBox 7.2.16, Windows hosts Oracle's September update, build 7.2.18 CVE-2026-108398 (.NET Framework) .NET Framework 4 on Windows, UMCI case tested on Windows 11 S Mode October 13 update, per-version KB Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.

10bk43n.text: What if your biggest SOC budget problem isn't how much you spend, but how much analyst time you lose? 9uomss.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 24, 2026Cloud Security / Vulnerability Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. "An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been." The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses. According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected. "On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory. "Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include - Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers Subscription keys Tokens used to call direct management APIs As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

1omkg7k.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 24, 2026Web Security / Vulnerability A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed. The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three. Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet. The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline. The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time. Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release. Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation. The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says. The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says. It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails. All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon. For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to: Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu. Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache. Update to a fixed release. The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough. This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

vu2wqr.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 24, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Vulnerability OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime. "It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X. The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption. The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software. Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service. The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation. To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it. "eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said. "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)." Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations. Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded. "Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands." This involves the following steps - An agent is tasked with finding new vulnerabilities in an application, or working off external sources of new vulnerability disclosures. Shirudo on the operator machine builds a security shield consisting of eBPF or application bytecode after reproducing and validating the exploit. The shield is delivered as signed .bee packages via an OCI-compliant registry. The Shirudo layer on each target pulls these .bee packages, validating each signature using TPMs to establish trust and safety. In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said. OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed. "We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before." "Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative."

1r1stu6.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The critical vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services. CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution. The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026. As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored. "N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity." CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China. "In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step." Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server. "In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root." Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network. The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, and AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge, revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft - AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization. AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain. AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access. In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework. "The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said. "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection." According to Datadog Security Labs, ARTEX also appears under other names like ScopeWeaver, LUCK — 自主资产控制台 (LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console), and 观澜SEC渗透测试平台 (Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform). In-the-wild activity involving ARTEX has also targeted several AWS environments with an aim to access financial data. Initial access vectors used in these attacks include compromised long-term AWS access keys and public Cognito user pools, with the latter being used to register an account, collect tokens, and enumerate AWS accounts. "In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents," security researcher Julie Agnes Sparks said. "The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like fund, invoice, billing, and LLC." Telemetry data gathered by Previdian from its sensors has recorded 52 HTTP requests containing explicit ARTEX markers between October 18 and November 15, 2026, from 10 source IP addresses. "Further investigation of these sources identified 3,651 related HTTP records involving application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal and attempts to retrieve sensitive configuration data," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said. "The most significant activity targeted Oracle WebLogic, Langflow, and Flowise, with additional payloads associated with Apache Struts, Log4j, and PHPUnit." Interestingly, one of the IP addresses associated with ARTEX activity, 31.22.91[.]156, overlaps with the AWS-documented campaign targeting AI infrastructure, including Langflow exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2025-3248. In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the latest fixes for the two flaws by November 26, 2026.

1qgj3h4.text: A threat actor breached the internal network of Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) and accessed two systems containing customer, employee, and contractor data. The attack exposed details of more than 1.5 million individuals before the company blocked access from external IP addresses and suspended the affected services. KEPCO is South Korea’s main electric power company and a state-controlled, major operator of the country’s critical infrastructure. The organization detected the attack on November 20, when it confirmed unauthorized access to its KEPCO ON electricity billing platform and its electronic procurement system (SRM). “On Friday, November 20, Korea Electric Power Corporation (hereafter KEPCO), led by President Kim Dong-cheol, confirmed that some customer information held in its IT systems had been exposed,” the power company states. “The company is making every effort to prevent harm.” ON is an integrated customer platform that allows customers to view and pay electricity bills. SRM is the company’s procurement system for contracting services. According to the announcement, published on Sunday, the following was exposed: for 650,487 KEPCO ON customers: names, ID information, phone numbers, addresses, bank names, bank account numbers, account holder names, card issuers, card numbers, cardholder names, and electricity charge and billing information. for 426,827 company representatives: names, ID information, email addresses, and company addresses. for 442,934 KEPCO employees: names, affiliation, employee ID number, mobile phone number, email address, company phone number. The company says the data breach resulted from “advanced technologies such as AI,” but it shared no specific details about the initial access method or the attack chain. KEPCO is notifying exposed individuals directly, has filed a report with the data protection authorities, and is coordinating with government and financial authorities to block abuse such as unauthorized transactions. Potentially exposed individuals are warned that the exposed information could be used for targeted phishing and impersonation. They are advised to report any attempts to the police or Korea’s Internet and Security Agency. It is also recommended to avoid installing unknown apps, entering information into suspicious forms, and sharing sensitive data or verification codes over calls or texts. A threat actor using the “Noiem” alias has claimed the attack and advertised the breach on a hacker forum on November 19, saying that they had KEPCO user data, supplier records, and bidding and contract documents. Noiem claiming the attack at KEPCO Source: dailysecu South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission separately confirmed that KEPCO received an email from a hacker claiming data theft on November 19. 13vrzvo.text: OpenRouter removed three AI providers from its platform after discovering that they had violated their stated data-handling policies and exposed sensitive data. The company also revoked Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution and notified all potentially affected customers. OpenRouter is an AI model broker that lets developers access AI models from different companies using a single API key. When an app sends a request, OpenRouter forwards it to a provider that runs the selected model and passes the answer back. Operational technology security company Dragos alerted OpenRouter after sending two million test prompts through the platform, each containing a unique tracking link or decoy credential, and detecting "activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed." Dragos discovered that, in some cases, those credentials were leaked to outsiders and used in the wild, indicating that the test prompts had escaped. “We observed activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed. Our seeded test prompts were used in attempts to access our controlled test systems and canary AWS accounts,” Dragos says. Discovering AWS key reuse Source: Dragos OpenRouter says there was no breach on its own systems, making the leak point at the provider level and leading to the decision to remove the three leaking inference providers: Together AI, Phala, and Novita. Another provider, Atlas Cloud, said it would voluntarily withdraw its models from OpenRouter pending security testing, following a third-party security incident. The other three published separate announcements responding to Dragos’ findings and explaining how the leaks occurred. Together AI said an AI coding agent exposed a repository credential on GitHub, allowing an unauthorized party to download stored prompt samples from June and July involving MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6. Phala said an attacker compromised a server processing DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests routed through OpenRouter between October 21 and 22, and possibly up to November 8, and obtained application credentials from affected virtual machines. Novita said a routing misconfiguration forwarded some MiniMax requests, including those sent through OpenRouter, to MiniMax’s official API between May 28 and November 11. All four providers are tightening security controls, strengthening their zero data retention or data deletion policies, and advising potentially impacted users to rotate any secrets that may have been exposed in the leaked requests. OpenRouter is also adapting Dragos’ tests for ongoing use to check whether AI providers forward or leak user requests/responses to third parties, and will require validation before restoring ZDR eligibility. ls9zcs.text: Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies. Azure API Management is a cloud service that lets organizations publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs that connect applications, services, and data. In an Azure Service Health security advisory (Tracking ID: MZK9-GH0) sent to customers and shared with BleepingComputer, Microsoft said it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day. "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue," Microsoft said in the advisory. According to Microsoft, the vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices. This access could have allowed attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets stored in the service. Microsoft said the following information may have been exposed: Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers Subscription keys Tokens used to call direct management APIs These credentials could potentially allow attackers to access additional applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions. Microsoft said it closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate. However, the company warned that its remediation would not invalidate customer credentials that may have been compromised before the fix was deployed. "This remediation blocks the unauthorized management-plane access path that could allow an actor to perform administrative operations, including secrets management, against Azure API Management services," Microsoft warned. "However, it does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed." The vulnerability affects Azure API Management Classic tiers, while Microsoft said APIM v2 tiers are not impacted. Microsoft urged affected customers to immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials, and review available logs for signs of unauthorized access. In a Reddit post, an administrator claimed their organization discovered the vulnerability after detecting unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token. "Our company has been fighting this for days, after discovering that someone logged into our keyvaults using a valid administrator token and not following the normal access pattern," the administrator claimed. The administrator alleged that attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances. According to the administrator, the legacy API did not generate logs that customers could use to detect the unauthorized access. They also alleged that Microsoft initially attributed the suspicious activity to leaked customer credentials before deploying a global fix. BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations. The vulnerability has also been linked to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. In a security advisory, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management. The agency said Norway's energy sector first discovered the vulnerability and that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected. Equinor disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, a day before Microsoft says it identified the APIM vulnerability. The company later announced that it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered. Skagerak Energi also reported an attempted cyberattack but said it had no impact on its operations and no evidence that information was compromised. While Microsoft says it deployed a remediation on November 19 that required no customer action, NSM's advisory warns organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update. The agency warns that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable and advises customers to contact their "service provider" if they have not received the update. It is unclear whether the runtime updates are separate from Microsoft's initial mitigation. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify credentials stored in their APIM instances. BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the attacks but has not received a reply yet. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1vupeek.text: LaLiga, Spain's top men's professional football league, disclosed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to users of its services and those of some affiliated clubs. According to the organization, the incident occurred between November 14 and 16, and the attacker extracted data from compromised systems. LaLiga organizes Spain’s top two men’s professional football divisions. The top league is one of the world’s most prominent football leagues, where clubs with a global audience, such as Real Madrid, FC Barcelona, and Atlético Madrid, play. On November 16, the organization’s security team identified the source of the unauthorized access and implemented measures to block the attack and stop the data extraction. “LALIGA was the target of a cyberattack on one of its technology platforms for fan services,” reads the announcement. “Between November 14 and 16, a cybercriminal gained unauthorized access to the platform and extracted personal data belonging to users registered for digital services offered by LALIGA and some clubs.” LaLiga underlined that the incident was confined to a specific platform and did not extend to other systems that support the running of the competitions. After implementing containment measures, LaLiga launched an investigation to determine the scope of the incident and introduced more thorough monitoring to detect future attempts to breach its systems. The football organizer also reported the incident to the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and filed a complaint with the National Police’s Central Cybercrime Unit. Impacted clubs were also directly notified, and actions to inform impacted fans are being coordinated. At the time of writing, no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack on LaLiga. BleepingComputer has contacted the organization to learn more about the attack and which clubs were impacted, but we have not received a response as of publication. nc5a7u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks. The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence. First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations. One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure. The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026. "The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions." The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN." One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity. It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response. The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark. Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below - Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB. Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII. What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth. "It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools. "We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

henuhc.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 23, 2026Cybersecurity News / Hacking A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open. This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need. The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week. ⚡ Threat of the Week Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines. 🔔 Top News Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks. Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners." Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue. New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account. GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild. Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser). 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars 6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers. 8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts. Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them. 📰 Around the Cyber World Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities.
