"Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping." One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background. Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API. One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities - Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store. One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed - A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager A downloader that directly downloads the main payload It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them. "Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]." The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically. "Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging." "When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon." Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely. Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels - Control, which is used to issue commands Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft - call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones contacts, to collect contact information device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands file_manager, to access the file system input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy push, to create and manage local Android notifications screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards toast, to display text messages on the device's screen twofa, to capture one-time verification codes uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian. "ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application." "Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest." ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data. "What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said. Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers. Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure. An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features - Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device Abuse accessibility services for full remote control Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password "The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said. "To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off." Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations. "By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

1rwvmxm.text: A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean. On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled. Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off. Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2. In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday. The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change. Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it. Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD. There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt. Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud. Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU. Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed. Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it. The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT. The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years. In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities. What to Do The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted. Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range. Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected. Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change. Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it: Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on. If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration. Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again. The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

91ebfq.text: Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027. The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters. The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it. Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence. Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents. In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system. Mapped onto security operations, the four stages look like this. Evidence collection. Querying the SIEM and EDR, pulling process trees, enriching indicators, gathering identity and cloud context. Analysis and verdict. Correlating what was collected, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether the alert is a real threat. Response recommendation. Proposing what should happen next, such as containing a host, resetting credentials or closing the case. Response execution. Actually changing something in the environment. This split gives security leaders a cleaner set of choices. A team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system. Human IN the loop vs. Human ON the loop Once autonomy is split by stage, teams need a shared way to describe how much of it each stage gets. A useful vocabulary comes from researchers at the University of Washington, who define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays. Level Human role What it means in practice L1 Operator The human directs and decides, and the agent carries out instructions L2 Collaborator Human and agent plan and execute together L3 Consultant The agent leads and checks in for expertise or preferences L4 Approver The agent works independently and asks for approval only in risky or predefined cases L5 Observer The agent acts on its own while the human monitors and can hit the stop button The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart. Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is. A highly capable agent can still run at L2 if the stakes call for it. Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic. Enterprises evaluating AI SOC vendors should make sure that both models can be applied as appropriate, across their entire operations. How to decide where and how much autonomy to grant an AI SOC The levels mentioned above tell you what the options are. Deciding where each SOC action belongs takes a rubric, and three questions do most of the work. Reversibility. If the agent gets this wrong, how quickly and completely can it be undone? Blast radius. How many users, systems or business processes does the action touch? Receipts. How strong and verifiable is the evidence behind the decision? An action backed by forensic proof of what was executed deserves more latitude than one backed by an LLM hunch about what looks suspicious. Scoring real actions against those questions produces a map that most security teams will recognize. Example action Reversibility Blast radius Suggested starting level Query SIEM, EDR or identity logs Nothing to reverse None L5, fully autonomous Enrich indicators and pull process trees Nothing to reverse None L5, fully autonomous Close a false positive with a full evidence trail Easy, the case can be reopened Low L4, autonomous with sampling review Open and route a ticket to an owner Easy Low L4, autonomous with sampling review Block a known malicious hash or domain Easy Low to medium L4, autonomous within defined policy Isolate a standard employee laptop Moderate One user L3 or L4, approval for sensitive groups Disable an account or revoke sessions Moderate One user, possibly many if a service account L3, approval required Isolate a production server or domain controller Hard Business-wide L2, human decides and agent executes The exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point. The rubric forces an explicit decision for each action, instead of a single policy that is either too loose for the dangerous actions or too tight for the safe ones. When human approval becomes a rubber stamp According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. It sounds like the safe choice, and in many cases it is. It also hides a failure mode that rarely gets discussed. Human approval is only as good as the context the reviewer receives. When an approval step arrives without clear evidence or criteria, reviewers start clicking through requests to keep the queue moving, and oversight quietly disappears. If the AI shapes how every investigation is framed, the human approving the final action is approving a conclusion they never saw being reached. Only when the reviewer can actually check the AI’s logic and work along with hard, forensic evidence that conclusively points in one direction or another, is the approval actually worth anything. In practice that means every approval request should show three things. The evidence the agent collected and where it came from. The reasoning that connects that evidence to the verdict. What the agent checked and ruled out along the way. A useful test if this is working, is time spent. If a reviewer cannot verify a verdict in a minute or two, the approval step is ceremonial and the team is paying for a human-in-the-loop without getting it. Autonomy you earn, autonomy you lose The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications gives this approach a name. It extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks and letting that autonomy grow as it is earned. Earning it requires criteria that are set before the pilot starts. Otherwise autonomy expands on vendor promises and gut feel. A practical set of graduation criteria for moving an action class up one level looks like this. Measured agreement. Track how often the agent's verdicts match analyst review over a defined period and alert volume, and set the threshold in advance. Dry runs first. Run new actions in a test mode that executes the logic but mocks every write, so the team sees what the agent would have done before it does anything. A complete evidence trail. Every decision at the new level must be auditable after the fact, including what the agent looked at and why it concluded what it did. A rollback path. Define how the action is undone and who owns that before expanding scope. Autonomy should also move down. A drop in agreement rates, a major change in the environment such as a new EDR or cloud migration, or a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. Teams that only ever ratchet upward are building risk they cannot see. Your SOC agent is an agent too Every level of autonomy granted to a SOC agent has a second effect. It raises the damage that agent can do if it is wrong, manipulated or compromised. Security leaders already feel this risk across the enterprise. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions. The lesson for the SOC is that autonomy itself is a risk factor, scored alongside the vulnerability. Treat the AI SOC agent the way you would treat a new privileged identity. Give it its own identity, never shared credentials. Scope its permissions to the actions it is approved for at its current level. Log every tool call, query and action in a form a human can review. Watch it with the same detections you would apply to a new admin account. A playbook for the next 12 months The move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. Security leaders who want the capacity gains without the incident that sets their AI program back a year can start with five steps. Inventory every action. List everything your AI SOC agent can do today, from read-only queries to response actions, and place each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric. Automate investigation aggressively. Evidence gathering and analysis consume most analyst hours and carry the least risk. This is where full autonomy pays off first. Gate disruptive response with real evidence. Keep approval on high-impact actions, and make sure every approval request carries proof a reviewer can verify quickly. Write graduation and demotion criteria now. Agree on the accuracy thresholds, test periods and rollback paths before the pilot starts, so autonomy expands on data. Govern the agent like a privileged identity. Scope it, log it and monitor it, because its autonomy is also its blast radius. Crossing the trust threshold Every SOC that adopts AI agents will eventually face the same question for each action. Is the agent's work trustworthy enough to act on without a human checking it first? A helpful way to think about it is a trust threshold. Below it, AI assists analysts, and humans still validate every conclusion. Above it, teams can safely hand off execution and supervise outcomes instead of steps. What moves an action across that line is depth and proof. An agent that can show what actually executed, where it came from and what it did, gives a human something real to verify, and gives the organization a defensible reason to extend its autonomy. Forensic-level investigation, the approach Intezer’s AI SOC is built on, is what moves an action across that line. That is what earned autonomy means in practice. The agent gets more authority one action class at a time, each step backed by evidence the team can inspect, and each step reversible if the evidence stops holding up. Note: This article has been written and contributed by Zev Schonberg, PMM at Intezer.

wo5w0u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Network Security / Vulnerability SonicWall has urged all customers still running Generation 6 firewalls to retire and replace them immediately and stop exposing the devices on the internet edge, citing security risks fueled by AI-assisted attacks. "Attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever," SonicWall said. "We expect internet-facing Gen 6 firewalls to be actively targeted. Treat any Gen 6 firewall still in service as a high-risk exposure, and migrate to a supported Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8." The affected products running SonicOS 6.x include - TZ350, TZ350W, TZ500, TZ500W, SOHO 250, SOHO 250W NSA 4600, NSA 5600, NSA 6600 NSa 4650, NSa 5650, NSa 6650 TZ400, TZ400W, TZ600, TZ600P, NSA 3600 NSa 3650 NSa 2650 SOHO, SOHO W, TZ300P, NSa 9250, NSa 9450, NSa 9650 NSv 10 to NSv 1600 (Gen 6 virtual) SuperMassive 9200, 9400, 9600, 9800 NSsp 12800, NSsp 12400 TZ300, TZ300W NSA 2600 In recent years, threat actors have increasingly targeted edge devices as a launch point to obtain initial access, even as the window between disclosure and confirmed exploitation has collapsed significantly, in part driven by threat actors' use of automation and AI to scan the internet for unsupported devices, analyze patches and vulnerability disclosure announcements, and build working exploits faster. According to Google Mandiant's M-Trends report published in March 2026, the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities has turned negative, reaching an estimated -7 days, meaning exploitation, on average, begins before a patch is available, down from 63 days in 2018 and -1 day in 2024. "This trend is compounded by threat actors' evolving interest in security appliances and networking infrastructure," Google said. "Because these assets provide critical inspection of data ingress and egress points, they grant significant visibility and permissions to those who gain access to them." Cisco Talos' 2025 Year in Review report has also found that 23% of CVEs discovered in the year directly impact network devices like VPN appliances, next-generation firewalls (NGFWs), load balancers, routers, and others. "Since these systems sit at the perimeter of enterprise environments, compromise may lead to direct access to the critical networks," Talos said. "This aligns with real-world trends from CISA'sKnown Exploitation Vulnerability (KEV) catalog, where exploitation consistently favors edge devices because they are internetfacing, often lag in patching, and provide direct operational leverage once compromised." With Gen 6 no longer being actively supported and receiving patches, even for critical flaws, users are recommended to follow the steps below without any delay - Inventory every Gen 6 firewall in the production environment and retire them. Prioritize units that are exposed to the internet or provide remote access. Replace them with a Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8 Contact an authorized SonicWall partner to plan the migration Until the firewall is replaced, it's advised to take the below actions to minimize exposure - Disable WAN management (HTTPS, SSH, and SNMP on WAN interfaces). Disable SSL VPN, or restrict it to known source addresses. Enforce multi-factor authentication on every remaining remote-access and admin account, and reset local passwords. Disable services and interfaces not in use. Monitor logs closely for unusual logins, configuration changes and traffic. "The risk to an unsupported firewall grows every day it stays online," SonicWall said. "One breach reaches everything. A compromised perimeter firewall gives attackers a foothold for credential theft, lateral movement and ransomware deployment."

ykgdri.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit. The activity involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root. "This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies," Cisco said in an advisory released late last month. "Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated." "An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device." Patches for the flaw were released in the following versions on October 21, 2026 - Cisco Expressway Series Release X14 and earlier - Migrate to a fixed release Cisco Expressway Series Release X15.5.3 and earlier - X15.5.20 In a report published Thursday, Russian cybersecurity company F6 said it observed what appears to be the first case of in-the-wild exploitation of the flaw to gain remote command execution on compromised Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices with root privileges after a PoC exploit became publicly available. "The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices," F6 said. "Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization's internal network." Following root access, the attackers are said to have undertaken efforts to move laterally across the network and use custom Python scripts to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive data. Analysis of the scripts indicates that they were possibly developed with assistance from artificial intelligence (AI) tools, given the presence of comments and descriptions of fixes. The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the activity - IP addresses geolocated: 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116 Presence of "wombat@127.0.0.1" in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices Python scripts staged in "/mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py" The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Users are advised to update to the latest supported version of Cisco Expressway, audit environments for signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, determine the scope of the attack, and block potential lateral movement vectors. "This incident demonstrates that compromise of a perimeter device can open a path for an attacker to an organization's critical systems," F6 said. "That means protection should therefore include not only timely vulnerability remediation but also properly configured segmentation and infrastructure monitoring."

yf0n2c.text: The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions - VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200 VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract) VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) "CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said. "Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local." An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW. "BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said. The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW. From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment. "The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW." Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities - SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance. BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server. SAWSNAKE, a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, thereby making it possible to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tokens, bypass multi-factor authentication(MFA), and impersonate any user. It's a Go-based port of an open-source Python script named "vcenter_saml_login.py." BEARBONES, a C backdoor based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server that's capable of bypassing system password authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from the temporary directory. LAZYBONES, a lightweight Go backdoor that uses Slack for command-and-control (C2) communications and has been previously deployed in a separate intrusion in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of a critical flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2025-22457, CVSS score: 9.0). It's suspected that Armory Castle had knowledge of the flaw prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026, with the recovered BONESAW binary containing a build timestamp of July 13, 2026. However, it's worth noting that build metadata can be modified before compilation. "After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, Armory Castle moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-<REDACTED>@vsphere.local," Google said. "Notably, Armory Castle enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. After enabling SSH, Armory Castle connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account." In the final stage of the attack, the adversary was found enumerating the ESXi file system, mounting Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and adding an SSH public key to the root account's authorized keys. It also conducted additional reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi file system, which were then archived and downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance for subsequent exfiltration. Furthermore, the attackers have been observed dropping LAZYBONES to a separate Linux appliance, which periodically checks for commands from a designated Slack channel, allowing it to perform command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. CVE-2026-123890 is the second vulnerability in a VMware product to be exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day this year alone. Late last month, CrowdStrike revealed it identified incidents where the hacking crew abused CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging flaw in VMware ESX, to reduce audit trail visibility. "BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days," Google said. "The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each." "The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting Armory Castle operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor's operational commitment to compromise high-priority targets."

tj4xh6.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Malware / Threat Intelligence Threat actors have been observed using the ROMULUS ClickFix malware delivery platform to deliver a previously undocumented remote access trojan (RAT) that shares similarities with CNCMachineRMS. "ROMULUS likely operates as a delivery service, distributing CNCMachineRMS and Legion Loader through separate chains while retaining ClickFix and signed binary sideloading techniques," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker, Nevan Beal, and Andi Ursry said in a report. ROMULUS was first publicly documented by Forescout Research last month, describing it as a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures to distribute malware families like Legion Loader (aka Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper). Attacks involving ROMULUS have also leveraged ChatGPT Custom GPTs as a pathway to direct unsuspecting victims to malicious sites that employ ClickFix lures to deliver a RAT payload by means of DLL sideloading. Interestingly, CNCMachineRMS has also been delivered via another malware loader called BabaDeda Loader through ClickFix attacks that employ DLL sideloading involving the legitimately signed IBM SPSS IDE executable. The latest findings from Blackpoint Cyber indicate that ROMULUS is distributing CNCMachineRMS alongside LegionLoader through separate infection chains. One of the payloads delivered through the ClickFix activity associated with ROMULUS is a malicious MSI installer ("IconEdit2Turb.msi") that's executed using "msiexec.exe" by means of a PowerShell command. The installer masquerades as Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool, while initiating a DLL sideloading chain to run a malicious DLL ("I++u.dll"). The DLL is designed to decode and run embedded shellcode responsible for launching CNCMachineRMS. It's worth noting that the RAT malware is the same final implant also distributed via the aforementioned ChatGPT Custom GPT lures. The trojan enables remote desktop control, screen streaming, microphone and camera capture, file management, and system reconnaissance. It's also equipped to run additional payloads on demand. Communication with attacker-controlled infrastructure takes place through DNS over HTTPS (DoH). "As attackers continue to change the applications and loaders used to distribute their payloads, the underlying malware architecture provides a more consistent way to identify related activity and understand the threats being delivered," Blackpoint Cyber said. The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of ClickFix-style campaigns that - Combine ClickFix with EtherHiding on more than 70,000 compromised websites to run JavaScript that interacts with a Polygon smart contract to fetch additional JavaScript that renders a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA prompt and ultimately deliver malware ("slaiclind"). Use fake Zillow apartment-review pages that serve a fake verification prompt to install NetSupport RAT on visitors' Windows computers. Employ a JavaScript-to-WordPress attack chain called TRUST#GRAFT that employs an unknown initial access method to inject JavaScript into WordPress sites that serves a fake Cloudflare verification prompt and then fingerprints the visitor and checks if the request is from an already authenticated WordPress administrator browser before uploading a malicious PHP plugin named Web Media Optimizer that's capable of injecting remote JavaScript into public pages and copying itself into the "mu-plugins" plugins directory for persistence. Use a sponsored Google search result for the keywords "amazon business" to a spoofed Amazon login page ("orders-amazon[.]com[.]advancedfences[.]com") with an embedded ClickFix command that uses the Window's built-in finger utility to initiate a multi-stage attack chain that leads to the deployment of the NetSupport Client remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool and a version of Lumma Stealer. Abuse Google Ads to direct users to an Anthropic Claude shared chat that stages a fake "Download Claude" page with ClickFix commands to trick Mac users into running a malicious command on their Terminal, resulting in the deployment of Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS) stealer. Use a typosquatted domain that employs a "House Wiring Scheme" theme ("veriffication-redirect[.]com") to serve a fake Cloudflare verification prompt, which utilizes clipboard manipulation to trick users into running a malicious command on the Windows Run dialog, which then retrieves next-stage Python payloads via DNS TXT records. This includes a previously unreported trojan called CrocoRat, along with a broader theft workflow targeting web browsers, stored credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and seed phrases on standalone systems. Directly contact targets via phone and convince them to open compromised WordPress sites that serve ClickFix lures to deliver malicious payloads via trojanized MSI packages masquerading as 3D PDF Maker Smart, Bitwarden VPN, and ESET Sysinspector, and execute them via DLL sideloading. Use a ClickFix variant called TerminalFix that instructs users to open Windows Terminal and run a command to deploy a Python-based tunneling implant using Lorem Ipsum Loader. The activity is being tracked as STAC4924. Use Google search ads for "claude mac" to a Bing search result, which then directs the victim to a compromised retail website before landing on a fake Claude download page. The bogus landing page employs another ClickFix variant called InstallFix to get Mac users to copy and run a malicious command on their Terminal. The crafty Google Search-to-Bing redirect and cloaking technique has been codenamed Adception. Use fake Cloudflare verification prompts on bogus sites mimicking gaming marketplace DMarket, Microsoft Office authentication in Czech ("login.microsoftofice[.]cz"), and U.K. retailer Howdens ("updates.howclens[.]com") to deliver CrashHandler RAT and remote access malware, including one that abuses the Stripe API as command-and-control (C2) to receive instructions and send back stolen information. In a report published last week, Huntress revealed that ClickFix broadened its scope beyond simple script or loader delivery into sophisticated attack chains that establish persistence, support lateral movement, and enable reconnaissance and credential theft, in some cases using steganographic tricks to hide malware and reconstruct them on the infected host. "Threat actors are using increasingly elaborate delivery methods, including browser-cache-seeded chains and executables reconstructed from data hidden in PNG files," Huntress researchers said.

x24j7j.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine. The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and found it works. There is no fix from Microsoft yet, and nothing shows the method has been used in a real attack. The technique does not work on every machine. It requires physical access to the computer and a Microsoft account accessible through the lock screen's recovery options, and it uses Windows' built-in screen reader, Narrator, to navigate the locked screen. In its test, the firm reached a point where it could run a program from the lock screen in a limited account that ThreatLocker identified as WSIAccount and said is "not an administrator account." The researcher's GitHub disclosure is a short post with a video and little written detail, so the clearest account of what the flaw does comes from the firm's independent test. Many Windows computers encrypt their drives with BitLocker, but in a common setup, that does not make them immune to this technique. A chip called the TPM unlocks the drive automatically when the computer starts, so by the time the lock screen appears, the files are already readable, and the bypass runs at that point. Microsoft's own TPM documentation describes this mode, in which the drive unlocks "without having to enter a PIN." FastUnlock does not break that encryption or recover the key. It runs on a computer that has already unlocked its own drive in the normal way, which is a smaller problem than cracking an encrypted disk, though still a real one for a machine someone else is holding. The conditions above, physical access and a reachable Microsoft account, are what put a machine at risk. No official list of affected Windows versions has been published, so treat any machine that meets those conditions as possibly affected until one is. What You Can Do Now With no patch available, the useful steps are about physical control and startup protection. Keep machines that can go missing out of the wrong hands. Lock away or closely manage laptops, shared desks, and front-counter computers that a stranger could reach. On sensitive machines, add a startup PIN to BitLocker instead of letting the drive unlock on its own. Shut down or hibernate devices when they leave someone's control. A startup PIN protects only a machine that has not yet started, not one already on the lock screen. Do not treat a locked screen on its own as enough. Microsoft's countermeasures guidance recommends using a startup PIN, along with shutting down or hibernating machines when faced with determined, hands-on attackers. Until an official fix or advisory appears, watch for one and apply it when it comes.

eyi2w7.text: The easiest way to fool someone is to give them something they already expect. A job offer. A message about a service outage. A familiar app. Nothing looks strange at first. And that's the problem. This week's stories show how ordinary things are being used to steal data, spread malware, and get people to hand over access.There's another shift worth watching. AI is making some attacks easier to run and harder to spot. Stolen data can now be searched like a shopping catalog. Phishing emails can be tested and rewritten until they get through. At the same time, researchers are finding that even powerful AI systems have safety gaps of their own.And while everyone is watching the new tools, the old problems haven't gone anywhere. Third-party breaches, years of hidden spying, ransomware, and security fixes still need attention. Some stories are clever. Others are painfully simple. Here's what caught our attention this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. Faster, more secure AI coding Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Neon, its latest frontier model capable of delivering reasoning faster and more cost-efficiently. According to the company's DeepMind division, it also produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). "Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost-efficient than large frontier models," Google said. "Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge." Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program. Major leap in AI cyber capabilities OpenAI has introduced GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol with a "significant jump" in cyber capabilities. "They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations," OpenAI said. "Like GPT‑6 Astra⁠, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework⁠." The company also said it has made defensive capabilities a core focus by allowing the models to write secure code from the start. The development comes amid a disclosure from the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI) that it developed a universal jailbreak against two pre-release versions of OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra in half the queries required for GPT-6 Astra, adding it identified a "substantial regression in jailbreak robustness relative to GPT-6 Astra." OpenAI has since addressed the regression. Urgent WordPress security update WordPress has released WordPress 7.1.5 with fixes for multiple security issues. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately," WordPress said. The patches have also been backported to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). Independent AI safety assessments OpenAI will embed independent evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot to help support its safety work. The embedded assessors will focus on model alignment and monitoring, training run monitoring, post-training alignment evaluations, and assessing "whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior." "Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases," the company said. "Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated." OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face. The pilot, however, limits how much researchers can disclose, with OpenAI reserving the right to redact evidence or confidential information to substantiate the outcome of their evaluations. $500 million ransomware extortion case Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, a Kazak national, has been extradited from Italy to the U.S. to face charges for his alleged role in a ransomware and extortion conspiracy that targeted U.S. schools, hospitals, and healthcare entities. "Khlynovskiy and other members of the '8-Digits Team' repeatedly targeted hospitals and schools, extorting victims and threatening to release highly sensitive information," said FBI Director Kash Patel. "This widespread extortion campaign resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands." The 8-Digits Team is said to have been affiliated with the INC and Lynx ransomware, and targeted victims in at least six states, including both schools and hospitals. Khlynovskiy was arrested in Italy in July 2025 while vacationing with his family. He is facing a maximum penalty of 27 years in prison on computer fraud, money laundering, wire fraud, extortion and identity theft charges. AI model extraction tactics exposed An exclusive report from Reuters has revealed that Chinese entities are adopting sophisticated methods to conduct distillation attacks against American AI models and use the outputs to train domestic rivals, according to a review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices, and government documents. "Chinese researchers [are] using U.S. models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models," the report said. AI-driven stolen data marketplace A criminal marketplace promoted on underground forums is selling data stolen from computers infected with infostealer malware, along with AI-written profiles of their owners, according to Hudson Rock. The seller has claimed registration for the service is open and free. "The reviewed listings present each computer with a description of its apparent owner, workplace, applications, and potentially valuable data," Hudson Rock said. "Buyers can search those descriptions using natural language and combine the results with filters such as country, operating system, and price. The result is a catalog in which a compromised machine can be presented as a clinic’s reception desk, a defense contractor's household computer, or a government employee's family workstation. The service is marketing the context around the stolen data as part of the product." North Korean ransomware campaign The North Korean hacking group known as Kimsuky group has been observed distributing the Funhouse ransomware via a malicious Hangul document that was disguised as a resume. "The Funhouse ransomware was identified as a variant of previously disclosed endpoint ransomware, and the tools used in this attack — such as Quasar RAT — as well as the overall attack chain shared numerous similarities with Kimsuky’s endpoint ransomware distribution cases observed since the first half of 2026," AhnLab said. Gemini chat retention extended Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change is expected to roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks. It marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period. "Even if Gemini History is turned off, future chats will still be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers," Google said in a revised policy update on November 17, 2026. The change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become increasingly capable. Anthropic and OpenAI, by comparison, have said they may keep temporary or incognito chats in ChatGPT and Claude for 30 days by default or up to 30 days. €11 million data privacy penalty Ireland's data protection regulator said it will fine Match Group €11 million ($10 million) as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request. The investigation was launched in January 2020. "The Download My Data tool was presented to Tinder users as a way to request a copy of their personal data," the Data Protection Commission (DPC) said. "It failed to provide users with all of their personal data. Certain categories of information were omitted without notice to the user, or provided in summary form only." In addition to the fine, Match Group has been ordered to bring its processing into compliance within three months. Rapid-fire domain impersonation Malicious actors registered one-letter lookalikes of new domains for a number of major brands a day after each real domain was registered. "Every lookalike was registered within the next working day of its authentic counterpart, which suggests the actors monitored new registrations made through brand-protection registrars," Broadcom said. "Most authentic domains appeared to be designed to host campaign sites for well-known brands, including Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald's, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi, such as patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, claims portals and legal settlements." The fake domains have been found to serve parked pages, deceptive search portals, and brand-themed blogs whose ads routed visitors to scam sites. The typosquatting campaign has focused on clients of two brand-protection registrars, Corporation Service Company (CSC) and MarkMonitor. EU targets Russian cyber operations The Council of the European Union has issued sanctions against Social Design Agency (SDA), a Moscow-based company known for running large-scale disinformation campaigns tracked as Doppelgänger. Also sanctioned are 24 individuals working for SDA and a pro-Russian hacktivist group known as NoName057(16). "SDA systematically manipulates the media and social media environment, spreads pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation and foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns," the Council said. "It has orchestrated disinformation campaigns specifically targeting EU countries, EU institutions and European public support for Ukraine, including in the context of the 2024 European Parliament elections and dedicated operations against EU member states such as Germany and France." Android espionage targets defense jobs An active GravityRAT surveillance campaign is using a fake recruitment portal ("recruitersglobal[.]net") to trick job seekers into downloading malicious Android apps. The campaign is targeting job seekers in India looking for work at foreign defense contractors. The activity has been attributed to Pakistani threat actors SpaceCobra and Cosmic Leopard. Once victims are lured into downloading the malicious app, it can steal contacts, call logs, and other sensitive information, and upload the data to the attackers' servers in less than 30 minutes. Over the past 12 months, GravityRAT has been detected across 14 devices from India, per Lookout. Similar variants of the malware have been tracked publicly as HeavyLift. Third-party breach exposes sensitive data DNS threat intelligence company Infoblox has disclosed a third-party breach that allowed criminals to access sensitive customer and staff data. The incident impacted a third-party data migration vendor that had access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, allowing the attackers to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This also includes employees' financial information such as direct deposit details, along with contact information, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. The scale of the compromise remains unknown, nor has the company named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked. Microsoft 365 outage fuels phishing Microsoft has identified a "coordinated, high volume" global phishing campaign designed to exploit the recent Microsoft 365 outage, which began on 11:20 a.m. EST on November 12 and lasted for more than 22 hours. The phishing emails were designed to exploit individuals' and employees' urgency to reconnect to Microsoft 365 services, attempting to trick them into clicking a malicious link and potentially capturing their credentials. The campaign targeted organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. "The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them," Microsoft said. "The available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext." AI-powered phishing evasion toolkit A new phishing kit called TheMailer is capable of orchestrating most elements of the attack through AI functionality, including designing email lures tailored to bypass content filters. The self-hosted phishing platform runs on AI models like Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, and DeepSeek, and personalizes lures for each mail provider and rewrites them until they bypass spam filters. The tool has been advertised on a cybercrime network since March 2026. "The clearest example of how far things have moved is TheMailer’s Inbox Loop," Varonis said. "It sends a test email and checks whether the test was filtered as spam. If so, the tool uses AI to rewrite the message and retry until it reaches the victim's inbox. TheMailer also writes HTML lures from short prompts, turns real brand emails into templates, tailors content to each mailbox provider’s filters, and strips 'AI patterns,' so the text is harder to detect." A lifetime license costs between $3,000 and $6,000 in cryptocurrency. New federal cybercrime disruption unit The U.S. Homeland Security Task Force's (HSTF) National Coordination Center (NCC) has announced the launch of the Threat Disruption Center, a new unit aimed at stopping the flow of victim funds to foreign criminal networks behind scams, cybercrime, and sextortion schemes targeting Americans. "It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible," HSTF said. "It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support." Five-year government cyber espionage Bulgaria has uncovered a five-year-long hacking operation that's estimated to have accessed tens of millions of pages of ​documents on a wide range of government databases. Since 2021 more than 130 GB, ​or 62 million pages, of documents had ​been downloaded. The Ministry for Innovation and Digital Transformation said there is no evidence that Bulgarians' personal data had been compromised. The agency has attributed the activity to "several international hacking groups" ​without naming one. The campaign was first discovered in August 2026 after a new national cybersecurity monitoring system was deployed. $40.5 million ransomware crackdown Ukrainian authorities, in partnership with the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have arrested four suspected members of an unspecified international ransomware organization alleged to be linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies across the world. The group has targeted organizations in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, logistics, financial, and critical infrastructure sectors. Some of the victims included Warren Oil Company, Maxxis International-USA, Newpark Resources, and Quantum Health. PNG-based malware delivery technique An evolving malware loader called BubbleLoader has been observed hijacking common benign software by hooking and adding two PNGs to convert it into a distribution mechanism for malicious payloads. Early BubbleLoader artifacts emerged in February 2026 and have been observed as recently as last month. "By patching and adding two PNGs to otherwise legitimate software, BubbleLoader is able to convert any executable to a malicious payload delivery mechanism," ReversingLabs said. "It targets common software as its host, such as WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, Firefox Launcher, and virtiofs. The patch is a series of instructions that are applied at the exact address of the host PE’s entry point. The entry point patch allocates memory and copies the PNGs into that location. The second, fake PNG houses both a small area of second-stage shellcode and the XOR-encrypted third stage. Once executed, this shellcode uses the first PNG as a rolling XOR key to decrypt the third stage. The third stage decrypts the final payload PE and then performs a reflective loading process that includes a set of anti-analysis features. The final payload is variable depending on the malware family being distributed." The strange part is how normal much of this has become. A fake email, a trusted tool, a third party nobody thought to question. Small things that can lead to expensive problems. The methods keep changing, but attackers still count on people being busy, systems being trusted, and warning signs being missed.That's it for this week. Keep an eye on the boring stuff. It has a habit of becoming the next big story.

1nkc3gn.text: PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server. Today's PHP releases fix the flaw, called phpAfterShell. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 scale by PHP's maintainers. Depthfirst, a security company, says it found the flaw and reported it to the maintainers. The October 21 PHP releases, which fixed two critical flaws known as PHP2Shell, do not contain this fix. Servers updated then remain affected until they install today's releases. Neither the maintainers nor the company reports any attacks using phpAfterShell. Who Is Affected and What to Do These releases are affected, according to the maintainers' security advisory: Branch Affected releases Fixed release PHP 8.2 Before 8.2.36 8.2.36 PHP 8.3 Before 8.3.37 8.3.37 PHP 8.4 Before 8.4.28 8.4.28 PHP 8.5 Before 8.5.13 8.5.13 PHP 8.6.0, also released today, includes the fix. The flaw is in the files session handler, which PHP uses by default. Sessions kept in Redis, a database, or another store are outside this defect, though each store's handling of a cut-off update needs its own check. Whether an attacker needs to log in depends on how the app exposes its session handling. On the path the company tested, the attacker uses upload progress, a PHP feature that records the progress of a file upload in the user's session. Where the feature is on, a multipart form upload that carries its field makes PHP write to the session before the app's own code runs. The app does not need an upload page, only any page that opens the session later. PHP 8.1 and older are end-of-life. The official end-of-life mitigation branches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are not affected, but older unpatched builds of those versions are, according to the company. The company's remediation guidance sets out these steps: Install the fixed release for your branch, as listed above. If you run PHP 8.1 or older, move to a supported branch. Rebuild any container images and redeploy. Check that the PHP version serving web requests is the new one. If you cannot update yet and your app does not use upload progress, set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the server's PHP settings, then restart the PHP workers. Also limit the untrusted data your app stores in sessions. Switching the feature off is not a full fix. It closes the upload path, but apps that put attacker-controlled data into sessions in other ways remain affected, the maintainers say. The maintainers listed the same setting on October 21 as a temporary measure for one of the PHP2Shell flaws. Servers that have kept it off since then still need the update. Moving sessions to a store that replaces records in one step also avoids this defect. The update is still the recommended fix for sites that keep the files handler. Linux distribution packages may include the fix without changing the PHP version number, according to the company, so the version number alone may not indicate whether a server is fixed. Once installed, the fixed releases empty the session file before each write and stop the write if that step fails. A cut-off write can still lose session data, but it can no longer leave old data behind for an attacker to use. The updates also switch upload progress off by default. The Hacker News compared PHP's source code for the October 21 releases and today's. The built-in setting is on in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and off in 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0. The release notes do not mention or explain the change. The sample php.ini files still show the old setting in a commented-out line. A php.ini file, distribution package, or hosting panel that switches the setting on will keep it on. Where nothing else sets it, apps that rely on upload progress will need it switched back on after the update. The same releases also fix other PHP security flaws. How the Attack Works The attack starts with the session write that upload progress makes before the app's code runs, Depthfirst's researchers say in their technical analysis. A PHP session file stores each value as a name followed by serialized data. Length fields in that data tell PHP where each string ends, and nothing in the file marks a write as finished. PHP locks the file while it writes, but the lock cannot undo a write that stops halfway. If the worker process dies partway through, the file can retain the start of the new data and the end of the old data. By setting the lengths in the new data, an attacker can make text that sat harmlessly inside the old data read as a separate record, including a serialized object. The next request that calls session_start() loads that record and creates the object. The researchers' public proof uses a harmless built-in object, stdClass, which appears in the session once the file is mixed. The emergency PHP2Shell fixes on October 21 addressed an earlier attack via the same step. "The original exploit stopped working, but the underlying problem was still there," the researchers say of the PHP2Shell patch. That exploit needed objects to become active while PHP recorded upload progress, so the maintainers limited which classes can load at that moment. The change did not touch the file write. The object data still reaches the disk and becomes active later, when an ordinary request calls session_start(). The attack depends on stopping the write at the right moment. The maintainers say one way is a hard memory-limit failure in another thread of a threaded PHP build, which can kill the process mid-write. Code execution then still needs a suitable gadget chain in the app, and the flaw can also corrupt session state. In the researchers' own Linux tests, PHP's execution timeout fired only after the write had finished, so they used an out-of-memory kill to stop the worker mid-write instead. The planted object appeared on the 11th attempt in a fresh run. That count measures getting the file into the right state on their servers, not how often code execution succeeds. Their own chain needed no gadget from the app, the researchers say. It used a second bug instead, memory corruption in one of PHP's built-in classes. They are holding back its details for coordinated disclosure and have not said whether that bug is fixed in today's releases. The same trick can also replace ordinary session values, such as who is logged in, their permissions, or a CSRF token, before the app checks them, the researchers say.

4xlpc9.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments, including CVE-2026-115560. The release of the patch follows an advance notice in which the project maintainers alerted users to multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions under specific conditions, including non-default configuration or uncommon setups. At a high level, successful exploitation of the defects could pave the way for remote code execution, session corruption, denial-of-service, memory corruption, or local privilege escalation. The list of vulnerabilities is as follows - CVE-2026-115560 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could result in remote code execution, file modification, session corruption, or denial-of-service. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in memory corruption and possible full remote code execution, as in the case of CVE-2026-109619. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability that could result in the execution of arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker. Successful exploitation requires an attacker's influence over the session data, an interruption at a useful point in the write, and an application with a suitable deserialization gadget chain. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests vulnerability that could result in execution of attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker without another user's interaction or a non-default PHP configuration. Successful exploitation requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens "php://input" without reading it fully, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections, and LSAPI. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in remote code execution on PHP 8.5 and later. Successful exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could cause an application's session cleanup to fail and potentially corrupt memory, crash a reused PHP worker, or potentially allow remote code execution. (Fixed in PHP 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code with their privileges on an affected deployment. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in local privilege escalation. Successful exploitation requires local code execution in an FPM worker, an affected pool with catch_workers_output enabled, the epoll event backend, and the ability to manipulate worker lifetimes and retain inherited pipe descriptors. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) Depthfirst, which has codenamed CVE-2026-126714 "phpAfterShell," has described it as a critical flaw that can enable a remote attacker to run arbitrary code on affected servers. "If a pwrite()/ftruncate() update is interrupted, PHP may leave behind a malformed session file that is later loaded by session_start(), yielding an arbitrary deserialization primitive," Depthfirst said. "Chained with another of our PHP-native deserialization-to-RCE findings, this leads directly to remote code execution."
