1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Employees should verify support requests through known internal channels before granting access. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. 1iw7jrm.text: A critical app used by thousands of Colorado residents for state services was taken down by a cyberattack last week. The Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) said the incident was discovered on the evening of November 18 and involved hackers breaching the myColorado app — which Colorado residents use for digital identification, document storage and accessing state government services. OIT shut down the app and began an investigation. The app is still unavailable as of Tuesday afternoon. The state noted that the app has 2.1 million users and the cyberattack likely involved the theft of data tied to nearly 150,000 people. Investigators declined to provide more information about what data may have been stolen by the cybercriminals. “We know how much Coloradans rely on these services, and we understand how this is frustrating and inconvenient. Protecting our users’ data is our first priority, and we will bring systems back online as quickly as we can once security is restored,” said Sarah Tuneberg, executive director of OIT. Colorado urged residents to bring their physical IDs if they are traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday. Those seeking to access state services can still do so through Colorado agency websites. The state previously dealt with major cyberattacks on the Department of Higher Education and ransomware attacks on several smaller municipalities. Several city and state governments are currently dealing with ransomware attacks and cyber incidents, including agencies in New York, Mississippi and California. On Friday, West Virginia’s legislature was knocked offline due to a cyberattack. Queens Public Library in New York City confirmed it has nearly recovered from a ransomware attack two weeks ago that shut down services at its 66 branches. The library, which serves the borough’s more than 2 million residents, has been forced to operate without digital services. The attack was claimed on Sunday by The Gentlemen ransomware gang — a cybercriminal group that claimed 398 attacks last quarter. The group far surpassed all other ransomware gangs with the amount of claimed victims, according to researchers at Halcyon. In Mississippi, Lauderdale County’s more than 70,000 residents were also impacted by a cyberattack on the sheriff’s office on Monday. The law enforcement agency said it was forced to take its systems offline after the cyberattack. Several services, including the inmate roster listing, are no longer available to the public. n99u9a.text: The director of the trailblazing California Privacy Protection Agency (CalPrivacy) on Tuesday announced his departure after nearly two years leading the organization as it implemented a first-in-the-nation platform allowing consumers to easily opt out of data sharing. Tom Kemp made the announcement in a LinkedIn post highlighting his work on the so-called Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform (DROP). The system is now used by more than 600,000 Californians who can block data sharing and foil data brokers with the push of a button. The platform debuted in January, but penalties for companies violating consumers’ data privacy wishes only went into effect in August. Each DROP user has, on average, forced more than 200 deletions by data brokers, Kemp said. He will begin a new position in January, but did not disclose any details about his new role. “I am proud that CalPrivacy under my tenure has made great progress in making it significantly easier for Californians to exercise their privacy rights, and that our work represents a case study of how to deliver innovative government services that can make a tangible difference,” he said. Under Kemp’s stewardship, CalPrivacy also led the push to pass two pieces of legislation expanding consumer privacy, lobbied against federal preemption of California’s tough privacy laws and oversaw the issuance of the largest fine in CalPrivacy’s history. The agency also adopted the country’s most comprehensive regulations mandating how industry deploys cybersecurity audits, risk assessments and automated decisionmaking technology. The latter refers to software, including algorithms and AI, that processes personal data to make decisions about individuals relating to employment and other significant events.

1ytsbhn.text: Rackspace is shutting down its Rackspace Spot cloud platform after a security breach allowed hackers to access customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets, giving customers until December 8 to migrate their services and download their data. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company announced the shutdown in a new security notification sent to customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, saying it had decided to discontinue the service after reviewing the incident. "Following a review of the situation, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the Rackspace Spot service. This decision is being made to provide a clear path forward for customers," reads the notification. Rackspace says the service will be permanently discontinued on December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time, when all remaining workloads will be terminated, and customer data will no longer be accessible. Customers have been instructed to retrieve their data and migrate their workloads to different platforms before the deadline. The decision comes after hackers breached Rackspace Spot on November 17 using compromised credentials, allowing them to create unauthorized pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Rackspace discovered the intrusion on November 18 following a customer report and disabled access to the platform's administration console while securing its infrastructure. Service was restored on November 21 following an extended outage. "An unauthorized party gained access to parts of the Spot platform and may have read cluster Secrets and files on storage volumes," Rackspace said. The company says the affected Spot environment is segmented from its core infrastructure and that it has not identified evidence of unauthorized access to its core systems or the environments of other Rackspace customers. Rackspace is now instructing all Spot customers to treat their API tokens, refresh tokens, kubeconfigs, and Kubernetes Secrets as potentially compromised, regardless of whether they previously received a breach notification. Customers have also been advised to review access logs dating back to November 16 and search for suspicious Kubernetes objects associated with the attack, including: IP address: 23.224.79.106 IP range: 23.224.0.0/15 Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe Customers urge Rackspace to reconsider The shutdown announcement has prompted disappointment among Rackspace Spot customers, with some urging the company to reconsider and offering to pay more to keep the platform operational. In a Reddit discussion, one customer said they believed users would be willing to pay higher prices to keep the service running. Other customers expressed similar concerns in a separate discussion, with some asking about affordable alternatives and others describing the impact the shutdown would have on their existing infrastructure. Others praised the service for its affordability, saying alternative cloud providers would be more expensive. Rackspace has not indicated whether it will reconsider the shutdown decision or offer customers additional time to migrate their workloads. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. aftgs8.text: A newly formed data extortion group named ‘Inception’ has been linked to a large-scale campaign that targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands and firms. The gang surfaced on November 17, claiming seven victims on its extortion site, including chip maker AMD, PepsiCo, Cigna Healthcare, AutoZone, and Lucid Motors, but none of them have publicly confirmed a data breach. However, cybersecurity company ReversingLabs has been tracking Inception gang's activity and says that it has been operating since late October. The security firm has confirmed the existence of 21 domains used for SSO phishing, 41 domains believed to be used in campaign infrastructure, and 4 other domains with suspected use. The researchers identified an extensive phishing infrastructure impersonating dozens of major corporations, including Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, Indeed, Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Twitch, Reddit, Nestlé, Anthropic, Nintendo, Starbucks, McDonald's, Paramount, and NBCUniversal. The existence of these domains is not proof that those firms have been breached, or even targeted yet, and none have recently disclosed cyberattacks or other related incidents. Homepage of the Inception leak site Source: BleepingComputer The campaign appears to rely on phone-based social engineering rather than email phishing, strongly resembling the tactics used by the infamous ShinyHunters extortion group. Inception is using legal-themed websites that imitate corporate authentication services, primarily Okta but also NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager. ShinyHunters link and denial One of those authentication providers, Okta, published a report yesterday linking Inception to O-UNC-053, a threat cluster it previously associated with ShinyHunters, which has been active since March. According to Okta, after law enforcement disrupted the ShinyHunters extortion group following the arrest of suspected members [1, 2], and the shutdown of the leak site, O-UNC-053 continued to register new phishing domains. In late October, the activity cluster launched its legal-themed campaign, and in mid-November, the Inception leak site went live, announcing victims that matched previous targeting. “This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” describes Okta. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation.” Inception was quick to respond and dispute the alleged links to other threat actors in an announcement on their extortion page. The threat actors claimed to operate independently and with no affiliation to any previous group, arguing that overlapping targets and the use of common domain registration and CDN services did not establish operational links. They also acknowledged that private tooling is circulating among independent threat actors, and using it does not prove affiliation. Threat actors' statement Source: BleepingComputer To defend against the latest Inception campaign, ReversingLabs recommends enforcing phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and strengthening help desk identity verification procedures. DNS, proxy, and identity provider logs dating back to October 21, 2026, should be carefully reviewed for signs of suspicious activity. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 124whbw.text: A bipartisan group of federal lawmakers on Monday sent a letter focused on security practices to several identity verification companies, citing a September breach that led to scans of more than 150 million people’s drivers’ licenses and other identification documents appearing for sale on the dark web. The breach of IDScan led to the theft of customer data stored in the company’s cloud platform, spurring an FBI probe and identity theft and fraud concerns for the vast number of Canadian and U.S. victims. The six lawmakers behind the letter pressured the identity verification firms to provide detailed answers about how they manage customers’ sensitive data and what they are doing to protect it against increasingly common and devastating hacks enabled by artificial intelligence. They cited not only the risk of fraud and identity theft, but also pointed to the fact that foreign adversaries are increasingly able to “infer Americans’ behavior through commercial data linked to government credentials,” said the letter, signed by Sens. Brian Schatz (D-HI) and Marcia Blackburn (R-TN) with four others from the Senate and House. “Given the difficulty of tracking these credentials and data sales, remedying this breach will pose substantial challenges even where no further crime is committed.” Brian Krebs, the independent technology journalist who first reported the IDScan breach in September, said on social media Tuesday that in the past couple of months he has found more than two dozen identity verification companies that store scanned IDs, often by default. Customers — the companies verifying users’ identities — often have to pay more to avoid the scans from continuing to be collected after verification, Krebs said. Cybercriminals on the Russia-tied dark web marketplace Nexus began exfiltrating the data more than a year before officials discovered the purloined information online, Krebs reported. In their letter, the lawmakers directed the identity verification companies to lessen risks by proactively hunting for system vulnerabilities, deploying zero-trust architecture and minimizing threats by limiting collection, sharing and storage of personally identifying information as much as possible. “This breach’s scale warrants additional attention to the data-handling practices of companies like yours,” a letter to IDScan CEO Jimmy Roussel said, noting that in addition to the identification documents nearly 600,000 medical cards, employment authorizations and other sensitive data was exposed. Many of the medical cards were for marijuana dispensaries, Krebs reported. The peddled license scans included ultraviolet, infrared and other detailed images, intensifying worries about how criminals may use it. A spokesperson for IDScan did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawmakers also emphasized that the personally identifiable information marketed by Nexus included scans belonging to high-ranking military and intelligence officials. “The consequences of this theft may be widespread and persistent,” the letter to Roussel said. “Given the difficulty of tracking these credentials and data sales, remedying this breach will pose substantial challenges even where no further crime is committed.” “Your duty to safeguard data is critical in light of AI-driven cyberattack capabilities, which may be utilized by cybercriminals for zero-day exploits.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

zqohex.text: Cybersecurity company Radware says attackers gained access to some of its customers' account details and cloud access keys through an unsecured internal Cloud WAF (Web Application Firewall) management API that was left exposed online. Founded in 1996 and headquartered in Tel Aviv, Radware now provides application delivery and DDoS protection services to more than 12,500 enterprise and telecom carrier customers worldwide. In a root cause analysis report shared by an anonymous source with BleepingComputer, Radware says it blocked the originating IP address and access to the internal management API. The company also revoked and replaced all internal account credentials after detecting the breach on Thursday, ten hours after the initial unauthorized API access. "On 19 November 2026, an unauthorized party accessed an internal-only Cloud WAF management API that was reachable from the Public Internet without requiring authentication," Radware said. "The confirmed information potentially accessed includes customer contact details, and for a subset of customers, the credentials configured for log export into their self-managed storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or SFTP)." The company added that the breach did not expose WAF traffic inspection, certificates, end-users’ data, customer application traffic, or cloud DDoS services and data. Customers advised to rotate exposed keys It also "strongly" advised affected AppSec (WAF, BOT) customers to rotate Cloud WAF log export credentials (including Azure Blob Storage keys or SAS tokens, AWS S3 access keys, or SFTP credentials) as soon as possible and review access logs on their cloud storage accounts for unexpected access since at least November 19. The company is still investigating the breach and whether any API keys or other customer information exposed in the incident were used without authorization, and said it has already received reports from customers about AWS alerts for an unfamiliar IP address attempting to access their log-export buckets. "WAF traffic inspection and protection have continued without interruption, and we have not identified an impact on the availability or protection of customer applications and services," Radware added. "We have found no evidence to date of changes to customer security policies or of access to customer application traffic." Radware has yet to issue a public statement regarding the incident or file a breach report with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. 1nuzx8w.text: Educational technology company Turnitin disclosed that it detected unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing systems and deployed its incident response plan. In a public statement, CEO Chris Caren says that the incident is being investigated with help from external cybersecurity specialists, and law enforcement and cyber regulators have been notified. Turnitin is a major education technology firm with a global presence, best known for its AI-generated writing detection, digital grading, academic research integrity checks, and examination proctoring. According to its website, its software is used in over 16,000 institutions across 185 countries and serves 71 million students. “We are writing to let you know that we recently identified unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing Turnitin systems,” reads the letter from the CEO on the platform's website. “Upon identifying the matter, we implemented our incident response plan, initiated an investigation with external cybersecurity specialists, and notified law enforcement and cyber regulators.” Turnitin says its systems are fully operational and safe to use, noting that the affected systems do not collect government identification credentials or institutional financial information. The company said its investigation into the incident remains ongoing and has not disclosed any details about the nature and scope of the unauthorized activity. If you have any information regarding this incident or other undisclosed attacks, you can contact us confidentially via Signal at 646-961-3731 or at tips@bleepingcomputer.com. Turnitin continues to monitor its systems for further unauthorized activity, indicating that it is still early to guarantee that the threat has been eliminated completely. The company has not disclosed whether any user data was accessed or stolen, when the incident occurred, and how many individuals might have been impacted. Regarding Turnitin service availability, the platform’s status page shows no incidents for November 2026, and the uptime history logs no disruptions. However, it's unclear whether it is safe to continue using the service and uploading sensitive data. As of writing, no ransomware groups have publicly taken responsibility for the attack at Turnitin. BleepingComputer has contacted the firm with questions about the incident, but a company representative said they have no additional details to share at this time. 1q1lqrm.text: The ShinyHunters extortion gang claims to have returned in posts on a new data leak site after a series of arrests over the past two months targeting alleged members. The new Tor site, launched on November 23, contains messages in both Russian and English announcing the group's return, distancing itself from alleged impostors, and denouncing a former member who was reportedly arrested and is cooperating with law enforcement. The site also includes two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys dating back to 2020, including one previously used to authenticate communications with BleepingComputer in August 2025. BleepingComputer confirmed that both messages were signed using known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang, confirming that the new operators have access to private signing keys historically used by the group. However, these keys do not confirm whether the individuals behind the new operation are the same people who previously controlled the group, as the keys have circulated among numerous people. The announcement follows a series of law enforcement operations targeting alleged ShinyHunters members after the group claimed to have breached FBI systems in September using an Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability. Later that month, Dutch police confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old Amsterdam man suspected of involvement with ShinyHunters, who was identified in media reports as Pepijn van der Stap, previously known online as Umbreon. In early October, another alleged ShinyHunters member known as Rey or Saif was reportedly detained in Jordan and is cooperating with law enforcement. Around the same time, Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested in Pennsylvania in an extortion investigation reportedly linked to ShinyHunters. After the arrests, ShinyHunters' main representative, who had regularly communicated with BleepingComputer and other media outlets, abruptly stopped responding, and their Telegram account was deleted. Soon after, the group's data leak site went offline. In the new statement, the purported ShinyHunters operators say they are returning after months of rumors and misinformation circulated about the group. "We’re finally back. A lot has happened recently, and there’s still plenty going on right now," reads the English announcement. "To be honest, there’s just too much nonsense going on. Everyone’s telling different stories, but no one is really explaining what’s been happening over the last few months." Post on the data leak site announcing ShinyHunter's return Source: BleepingComputer The operators of the new data leak site say they will communicate exclusively through the Exploit hacking forum account, which they claim to have controlled since 2020, and through the new Tor site. The statement also addresses the reported arrest of a hacker and ShinyHunters member known as Rey, Dedale, or Saif, who was reportedly detained in Jordan in late September. According to the announcement, Rey previously collaborated with ShinyHunters but began operating independently, creating Telegram channels without the group's approval. "As far as we know, he has already been arrested and is now "actively cooperating" with the authorities," reads the English message. "We already rotated the PGP key that Rey used for DLS, since it has most likely been compromised." The message also mocks two other individuals reportedly tied to the ShinyHunters investigation, Umbreon and Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky, referring to their arrests. "It was a pleasure working with you. And it’s truly a shame that our guys got caught because of such silly mistakes, ones that could easily have been avoided if you fools hadn’t gotten involved with the wrong people," reads the post. The operators say they plan to launch a new CDN for hosting stolen data and will no longer use any of the existing backup servers. Old PGP keys used to authenticate new site To attempt to prove their legitimacy, the operators published two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys created in January and August 2020. The keys have the following fingerprints: ShinyHunters RaidForums PGP key: 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3 ShinyHunters Empire Market PGP key: 828537C15F43F135A8317153CD16A1660CC7CE51 BleepingComputer verified that both messages were signed using these known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang. November 2026 message signed using historic ShinyHunters PGP key PGP uses a pair of cryptographic keys: a public key that anyone can access and use to verify a message or data, and a private key used to create signatures. The private key must be kept secret to prevent others from impersonating the key's owner. BleepingComputer previously verified a message received from ShinyHunters on August 26, 2025, using the 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3 public key. Successful verification of the November message with that same public key shows that whoever signed it had access to the same private signing key used in the earlier communications, linking it to the ShinyHunters operation behind the widespread data theft attacks in 2026. However, both historical keys were revoked in March 2026, when ShinyHunters announced a replacement PGP key with the fingerprint F4953411767DE71BEDCDABCB76F4E26F7A20978A. At the time, the group used both 2020 keys to authenticate the replacement and stated that the older keys would no longer be used for communications. Despite this, the November 23 announcement once again uses the two revoked 2020 keys to authenticate another new PGP key, 27DA9D5B183247CADFC322880ABC63E30F73822E. However, none of the November messages examined by BleepingComputer were signed using the March 2026 replacement key, leaving it unclear whether the new operators also have access to that private key. Because it was rumored that numerous people had the original 2020 keys, these unfortunately do not prove with certainty that the ShinyHunters group has returned or that the brand has not been revived by imposters. ndc7by.text: The European Commission, the European Union's main executive body, has confirmed that attackers breached its EU Academy online learning hub and stole the personal data of an undisclosed number of users. This follows the Commission's Thursday disclosure that hackers breached its systems on October 22 using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework, causing service disruptions that also affected its internal Sysper HR platform. "As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several ​applications and most of them have since been restored. The investigation is still ongoing," spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters at the time. "We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings as they come. We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole." While the Commission said it hasn't received a ransom demand and has yet to attribute the attack, Regnier confirmed in a Monday press briefing that the attackers also breached the EU Academy platform, used to learn more about EU policies and follow EU online courses. Regnier also confirmed a data leak following the EU Academy incident, which is still under investigation and has affected users' personal information, including their names and email addresses. "And as a precautionary measure, given that the fact that there is a data leak that is confirmed including names and email addresses,today there was a message to all users on the EU academy website," he added. "This is definitely a cyber attack, a cyber campaign that was targeted against the Commission via an AI assisted tool. When it comes to the attribution, we would need the investigation to be concluded to be able to find out who is behind this." The Commission has also published a notice on the EU Academy website about this cybersecurity incident, informing users that public access to the platform has been disabled and warning them to be suspicious of unsolicited emails or messages that may be part of potential phishing attacks. The European Commission disclosed another data breach in February after discovering on January 30 that a mobile device management platform used to manage staff devices had been compromised. More recently, it disclosed an additional incident on March 27 after BleepingComputer reached out for confirmation that the Commission's Amazon cloud environment had been breached. The EU's Cybersecurity Service (CERT-EU) later attributed the March cloud hack to the TeamPCP threat group and said the resulting breach exposed the data of at least 29 other Union entities. These recent security breaches follow the Commission's January 20 proposal for new cybersecurity legislation to strengthen defenses against cybercrime groups and state-backed actors targeting Europe's critical infrastructure. fxk3gl.text: Threat actors have exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise two dozen Check Point Security management servers in an ongoing campaign targeting 22 organizations. Threat intelligence firm GreyNoise detected the activity, noting that it resembled cyberespionage operations, although the attacker's motivation could not be conclusively determined. The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232 during the post-compromise stages. The vulnerability is an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. Check Point warned about the flaw in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day. The researchers also observed attempts to exploit CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF). GreyNoise recorded over 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 file-related activities, such as: Stealing firewall databases, credentials, configuration data, and internal certificate authority files. Generating a new certificate in one victim's environment. Unloading security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections. Conducting internal network reconnaissance and attempting lateral movement. Targeting additional enterprise systems, including Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966), Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2024-21893), VMware vCenter (CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048), Microsoft Exchange (CVE-2021-26855/34473), and Microsoft Netlogon (CVE-2020-1472). Overview of the attacks Source: GreyNoise On October 26, the attacker performed a bulk certificate management operation across all 24 compromised Check Point servers, which failed, but still helped GreyNoise identify victims. Τhe researchers assess that GT13 operated an AI-powered offensive tool, based on behavior, observed automation, and custom tooling, but the use of AI in this campaign remains unconfirmed. Although GreyNoise lost visibility into the campaign operations on November 2, the researchers believe it could still be ongoing and have notified international government partners and CERTs to alert impacted organizations. The company also shared indicators of compromise (IoCs) that could help identify additional intrusions or block future attempts. BleepingComputer has contacted Check Point to ask if they have better visibility into those attacks and which flaw was exploited for initial access, and we are waiting for their response. ngwx2k.text: A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus. Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025. Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to harvest email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations. The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). "While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments." This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives. Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel. This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. "This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said. As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia. A Windows backdoor, KuboShell, uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network. "On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained. "KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token." Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server. It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds. Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process - PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown. "We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said. The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe." "Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention." "If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

3zxzuq.text: Some donors to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace had their information leaked due to a cyberattack on a third-party vendor named Soapbox Engage. The organization sent emails to past donors on Friday warning of the data breach, writing that the incident occurred on October 28. The threat actors were removed from the vendor’s system on October 30, they said. Carnegie Endowment for International Peace spokesperson Sharmeen Aly confirmed to Recorded Future News that the vendor was Soapbox Engage — an online fundraising and engagement software platform for nonprofits. Carnegie uses Soapbox Engage for online donations. The hackers stole names, email addresses, phone numbers and giving history. “Due to an integration with Carnegie's database, the unauthorized users were able to temporarily gain access to contact information maintained by Carnegie,” Aly said. “Based on our investigation, a small percentage of our database was affected. No full credit card numbers were exposed.” Aly added that the organization notified everyone in their database about the breach due to European data privacy laws. Carnegie hired a cybersecurity firm to confirm the hackers were removed from the system. Aly did not say how many people were impacted by the incident. Founded in 1910, the think tank currently employs more than 200 experts. The institute supports research efforts, diplomacy and more. In its last financial statement, the non-profit declared more than $522 million in assets and an operating revenue of about $51 million. Soapbox Engage did not respond to requests for comment but the incident coincides with the disclosure of data breaches and cyberattacks by multiple digital donation platforms. Fundraising software company DonorPerfect said it was impacted by a security incident last week, and on Friday GoFundMe said it identified a cybersecurity incident where hackers breached their systems in two separate attacks in October and November. GoFundMe reported the cyberattack to law enforcement. “We have reviewed the data involved, and determined it included limited personal information such as names, postal addresses, phone numbers and, for some, dates of birth or other information provided voluntarily in registration forms,” the company said. No card numbers or bank details were exposed and GoFundMe said they “addressed the known methods of unauthorized access, disabled unauthorized accounts, and are actively monitoring for further suspicious activity.” In its statement, GoFundMe said the recent attacks on other fundraising platforms were evidence that organizations had to do a better job of protecting donor information. “To help prevent something like this from happening again, we are identifying opportunities to further strengthen the safeguards protecting our platform and are using those findings to guide additional security improvements designed to help prevent similar incidents,” the company said. The Nonprofit Times news outlet reported that the recent attacks on the fundraising platforms appeared to be coordinated and at least one incident involved the theft of funds.
